Overarching arguments and design rulings:
- Layering: the member layer (cosponsorship and press) stays independent. The staffer network is its own layer below members, with members as attachment points and no member-member edges. Lobbyists enter as outsiders via revolving-door edges. Layers combine only at analysis time in a multiplex, never inside each other's weights. Multiplying the cosponsorship adjacency into staffer weights is banned as double-counting and as a comparability contaminant (same failure class as the LD-2 circularity).
- Edge rule (OVERLAP): a person-person edge requires real temporal overlap in the same container, weighted by overlap duration times container kappa. Sequence across offices is a trajectory property (ordered stints, office-to-office moves), never a person-person edge. Every build must emit a negative control counting edges a build without the overlap test would produce.
- Education is excluded (weight alpha=0 kept in code), so the final weight reduces to W = w_work, purely staffer-derived and therefore comparable to the bill graph.
- Non-circularity: LobbyView network.csv, lobbyview_network_member.csv, our_network_*.csv and bill_lobbying_sidecar.json are banned as circular. LD-2 filings never name members, so lobbied-member edges are joins by construction; zero influence or predictor phrasing on LDA-derived edges is a language law (I-15). Revolving-layer join on lda_source_person_id verified not circular.
- Inference is never merged with observation: predicted destinations live in a separate exploratory tier, to avoid self-confirmation.
- Identity: STRICT-BIOGUIDE (no fuzzy member joins), declaration-directed matching, paired control arms per widening tier with a positive control, and coverage alarms with match-rate floors that abort fail-closed.

- Whether committee payrolls (missed by a prior parse, "committee membership does not exist on disk" was wrong) are the main source of cross-party ties, since personal offices are partisan silos. Committee kappa is treated as load-bearing for whole-graph connectivity; the plan asks whether committees are what hold the graph together.
- Side (maj/min/bipartisan/unknown) is four-valued because committee staff are mixed; the kappa=0.40 opposite-side row is reachable, not structurally dead.
- Centrality is computed per connected component, since eigenvector centrality is ill-defined on fragmented graphs and PARTIAL_NULL at L3/L4 is read as fragmentation, not iteration limits.
- Interval algebra: union before intersection, because naive pairwise summation invents about 13.7M co-tenure days (1.0%).

works.title: Breaking the Sorting Barrier for Directed Single-Source Shortest Paths
works.summary:
Duan, Mao, Mao, Shu and Yin (arXiv 2504.17033v2, 2025; Paul's bib lists it as STOC 2025) give a deterministic single-source shortest-path algorithm for **directed** graphs with real non-negative weights that runs in O(m log^(2/3) n) in the comparison-addition model. It is the first to beat Dijkstra's O(m + n log n) on sparse graphs. The method combines Dijkstra with Bellman-Ford through a recursive bounded multi-source routine (BMSSP). FindPivots shrinks the frontier to at most |U|/k pivots, and a block-list structure sorts only partially, with k = log^(1/3) n and t = log^(2/3) n. The result covers distances only, with no full distance ordering. It is purely theoretical: there is no implementation, and the constant C is never given.

For Paul's systems this is a speed result with very little to transfer. Every route engine as built is either tiny (533 members, an O(N^2) array scan in the dashboard), a point-to-sink query that stops early (staffer closeness routes, bidirectional, plus Yen alternatives), or an integer-weight search (overlap routes). The paper's bound covers full single-source distances on sparse graphs with real weights, so none of these uses fits its model. The one real link is Assumption 2.1: the paper breaks ties by lexicographic order on (length, hop count, predecessor), which matches the staffer router's (cost, steps) tie rule. On latency, the staffer-network lane found the bottleneck was memory (pair_cache), not the heap's log n. ALT landmarks remain the deferred lever, and this paper does not replace them. While checking the dashboard's 'provably optimal' chain, I found a possible problem with edge direction (see flags). It is UNVERIFIED.
works.question: Can single-source shortest paths (SSSP) on directed graphs with real non-negative edge weights be solved faster than Dijkstra's O(m + n log n) bound on sparse graphs, in the comparison-addition model, and can the Omega(n log n) sorting barrier be broken for this problem?
works.method: Deterministic algorithm design plus worst-case running-time analysis. The core procedure is a recursive bounded multi-source shortest path routine, BMSSP(l, B, S) (Algorithm 3, p. 10). It uses FindPivots (Algorithm 1, p. 6), a base case that is a mini-Dijkstra (Algorithm 2, p. 9), and a partial-sort block-list data structure D (Lemma 3.3, pp. 6-8). Parameters are k = floor(log^(1/3) n) and t = floor(log^(2/3) n), with recursion depth ceil(log n / t) (Sec. 3.1, p. 4). Correctness is proved by induction on level l (Lemma 3.7, pp. 12-13). Time is bounded in Lemma 3.12 (p. 14).

findings.finding: Main result: a deterministic SSSP algorithm for directed graphs with real non-negative weights in time O(m log^(2/3) n), the first to break the O(m + n log n) bound of Dijkstra on sparse graphs.
findings.numbers: O(m log^(2/3) n)

findings.finding: The result is also the first deterministic algorithm to beat O(m + n log n) for SSSP even on undirected graphs, since the prior O(m sqrt(log n log log n)) SSSP algorithm of Duan, Mao, Shu, Yin (DMSY23) is randomized.
findings.location: Sec. 1, p. 2 (remark after Theorem 1.1); DMSY23 cited on p. 1
findings.numbers: DMSY23: O(m sqrt(log n log log n)) randomized, undirected

findings.finding: Dijkstra is optimal if the output must include the vertex ordering by distance (Haeupler et al. 2024), so the improvement applies to distances without a full ordering.
findings.location: Sec. 1, p. 1 (citing HHR+24); Sec. 3.1 p. 4 ('without necessarily recovering a complete ordering')

findings.finding: Key idea: shrink the frontier. For a bound B, the frontier S is reduced to pivots of size at most |eU|/k, where k = log^(Omega(1)) n. Each pivot roots a shortest-path tree of at least k vertices.
findings.location: Technical overview, Sec. 1.1, p. 2; FindPivots Lemma 3.2, p. 5
findings.numbers: |W| = O(k|S|); |P| <= |W|/k <= |eU|/k; time O(min{k^2|S|, k|eU|})

findings.finding: Per-vertex running time is reduced from Theta(log n) to log n / log^(Omega(1)) n through divide-and-conquer over log n / t levels.
findings.numbers: log n / log^(Omega(1))(n) per vertex

findings.finding: Parameter choice that yields the final bound: k = floor(log^(1/3) n), t = floor(log^(2/3) n), recursion level l = ceil(log n / t).
findings.location: Sec. 3.1, p. 4; Lemma 3.12 final statement, p. 14
findings.numbers: k = floor(log^(1/3) n); t = floor(log^(2/3) n); l = ceil(log n / t)

Chen maximizes on-time arrival probability under a travel-time budget with stochastic link times (MRP-TS), not the dashboard's product of independent per-edge probabilities; Duan only bounds exact deterministic SSSP cost.
Empirically compares Dijkstra, A*, BFS and Greedy Best First on small 2D grids; covers the heuristic/goal-directed family that Duan's exact worst-case result does not.

Multi-Objective Path-Based D* Lite (incremental multi-objective replanning) covers dynamic and multi-objective cases that Duan's static single-objective SSSP does not. The analyst's claim that it is cited for a Pareto cosponsor route finder was not found in fec/surfaces.

works.title: A Systematic Review and Analysis of Intelligence-Based Pathfinding Algorithms in the Field of Video Games
works.summary:
Lawande et al. (2022) call the paper a systematic review, but it is really a benchmark of four algorithms on one setup: BFS, Dijkstra, A* and Greedy Best First (GBF), each run once on Unity square grids from 4x4 to 32x32, with and without obstacles. It reports no search protocol, no repeated trials, no hardware details and no measured memory, so its memory rankings and the Table 5 citations (several of which do not match the claims) cannot be relied on. The usable results are narrow. With no obstacles, GBF is fastest at every size; Dijkstra is 2.8x to 21.6x slower than GBF, and all four find the same path length. With obstacles, GBF stays fastest from 8x8 up, but its paths get longer (37 vs 31 at 16x16, 81 vs 75 at 32x32). A* expands fewer nodes than Dijkstra on the larger grids (587 vs 754 iterations at 32x32) and still returns the optimal length. D* and D* Lite are only described, never tested. The proposed GRIN_PF is just a loop that runs the four existing algorithms.

What this means for the system as built is mostly a check on design choices, not new evidence. The one sharp bearing comes from the paper's GBF-with-obstacles result. The dashboard's recruitment path first runs an exact max-product Dijkstra backward from the target (`distToTarget`), then walks forward greedily, choosing at each hop the neighbour with the highest edge probability times its precomputed reliability to the target. That walk is optimal only while the precomputed reliabilities are exact. Once a user drops members, the walk skips them but the reliabilities are still computed through them. The walk then becomes a greedy best-first search on an out-of-date estimate, which is the case where the paper shows longer, non-optimal paths. Terrier's walk router already does textbook A* with an admissible straight-line estimate, which is the setting where the paper's A* result applies best. For the non-spatial social graphs, the paper offers no usable heuristic.
works.question: Which of four pathfinding algorithms (Dijkstra, A*, Breadth First Search, Greedy Best First) performs best on 2D square grids of size 4x4 to 32x32, with and without obstacles, in terms of execution time, total iteration blocks, computed blocks and shortest path length, so that game developers can choose one? Secondary: how do the families compare in the literature on memory and time (Table 5).
works.method: Implemented BFS, Dijkstra, A* and Greedy Best First in Unity (Algorithms 1-4; the "GRIN_PF" Algorithm 6 is a harness that loops over these four). Per run recorded: total iteration blocks, total computed blocks excluding the shortest path, execution time in ms, and shortest path length in blocks (Section 5, p.19-20). Results compared as within-size rankings and narrative (Section 6, p.23-26). Theoretical side: asymptotic time/space table (Table 2, p.14) and a pairwise literature comparison table with category, time, memory, implemented yes/no, and cited source (Table 5, p.26-27). No statistical tests, confidence intervals, or repeated timings. Memory was not measured.

works.title: Most Reliable Path-finding Algorithm for Maximizing On-Time Arrival Probability
works.summary:
Chen, Shi, Zhang, Lam, Li and Xiang study a road-routing problem. Each link has a random travel time, and the goal is the path with the highest probability of arriving within a fixed time budget b, P(T <= b). They treat path times as normal, so this means minimizing (b - mean)/SD. Because path SD is the square root of summed variances, the objective is non-additive, and the authors state that Dijkstra-type methods cannot solve it. Their exact two-stage algorithm, MRP-TS, works as follows. A deterministic least-expected-time search first fixes the risk regime. Mean-Budget dominance with multi-criteria label-setting then finds the optimum. They check optimality by matching an independent multi-criteria A* on the same budgets. On Wuhan taxi data (19,306 nodes, 2009 morning peaks), the best path changes with b: a short budget picks a high-variance path and a long budget picks a low-variance one. MRP-TS runs in milliseconds, about 750x faster than the label-correcting benchmark on Chicago. Links are assumed independent, and the authors name correlation as the main open limitation.

What this means for Paul's system is narrow. The dashboard's recruitment chain (`make_dashboard_html_00.tpl:735-757`) cites this paper as grounding for its max-product path. That path is a different problem: the classical product-of-independent-probabilities path, which is additive in -log p and correctly solved by Dijkstra. This paper is about deadline-reliability, which is the case Dijkstra cannot handle. So the citation supports the word 'reliable', not the method. The paper's useful lessons are elsewhere. Exact optimality claims should be checked against a second algorithm, as Chen et al. do. Products of independent per-hop probabilities overstate certainty when the hops are correlated. And a true deadline or variance penalty on a recruitment chain would need label-setting, not Dijkstra. Nothing here concerns lobbying, legislators or elections.
works.question: How can the most reliable path, the path that maximizes the probability of arriving on time for a fixed travel-time budget, be found exactly and efficiently in large road networks with stochastic link travel times? (Abstract; Sec. 1, pp. 3-5.)
works.method: Two-stage exact algorithm, MRP-TS. Stage 1: a deterministic A* or Dijkstra search finds the least expected time path, which gives an upper or lower bound on the optimal reliability and sets the risk regime (Prop. 2). Stage 2: a multi-criteria label-setting procedure, MRP-RS for risk-seeking (fixed confidence level, Sec. 3.1) and MRP-RA for risk-averse (adaptive confidence level starting at 0.999, z = 3.5, with an admissible heuristic h(i), Sec. 3.2). Risk-neutral cases return the least expected time path directly. Optimality is argued through Props. 4-5 and Lemmas 1-3. Complexity is analyzed in Sec. 3.3. Benchmarks: the authors' improved multi-criteria label-correcting BSP-LC (Nie and Wu 2009 extended with a bi-criteria method, Appendix B, valid only for normal times), and multi-criteria A* from Chen et al. (2013a) used to check that MRP-TS returns the same paths. Implemented in Visual C#, one core of a 2.0 GHz i7 laptop, Windows 7. Identification strategy: not applicable; this is an algorithmic and computational paper with no causal design.

findings.finding: The most reliable path is non-additive, so deterministic shortest-path algorithms cannot solve it; FSD label-correcting (Nie and Wu 2009) generates an exponentially growing number of non-dominated paths.
findings.numbers: none

findings.finding: A two-stage exact algorithm (MRP-TS) first estimates the reliability range from the least expected time path, then applies M-B dominance with multi-criteria label-setting. Optimality is proven under admissible heuristics.
findings.numbers: Adaptive confidence level starts at 0.999 (z = 3.5) for the risk-averse procedure

findings.finding: Normal distributions fit only a minority of link travel times on their own, while lognormal fits best overall. No single distribution fits all links.
findings.numbers: Significant fit at 5%: normal 58.85%, lognormal 81.64%, gamma 67.19%. Best-fit shares: lognormal 50.29%, gamma 30.25%, normal 19.46%

findings.finding: Link travel times in the Wuhan network are highly variable, with 10.25% of links congested (below 20 km/h).
findings.numbers: Average coefficient of variation 0.37; 10.25% of links under 20 km/h

findings.finding: Normal approximation of path travel times is good enough for route guidance. Accuracy is higher at the 10th percentile than the 90th, because of positive skew, and improves with path length.
findings.numbers: Monte Carlo ground truth on 100 paths: 98.3% accuracy at 10th percentile, 94.9% at 90th percentile

findings.finding: A worked O-D example shows the chosen path changing with the budget b: a short budget selects a high-variance path, a budget equal to the least expected time selects the mean path, and a longer budget selects a low-variance path.
findings.numbers: b = 2301.4 s (Path 1, risk-seeking); b = 2630.9 s (Path 3, least expected time, reliability 50%); b = 2875.5 s (Path 2, risk-averse)

Duan et al. speed up additive single-source shortest paths, which is the problem class the -log p chain and the staffer router belong to. Chen's objective is outside that class.

Both prune dominated partial paths with multi-criteria labels to get non-dominated path sets (MOPBD* path-based expansion vs M-B dominance label-setting). Ren also offers a sub-optimal variant that approximates the Pareto front, so it shows both the exact and approximate options relative to the lambda-scalarized front in cosponsor_route.py.

Lawande reviews heuristic pathfinding (A*, D*, HPA*). Chen's MRP-RA needs an admissible lower-bound heuristic for optimality (Prop. 5), which bears on Paul's wish for heuristic-augmented A* in the routers (both use heuristic 0). Lawande's text does not itself discuss admissibility.

works.title: Shortest Path Algorithms for Social Network Strengths
works.summary:
Ahmad, Ahmad and Vijay compare two ways of finding a social-search path between a source and a target. The first is plain Dijkstra, measured in hops. The second is the "strongest path" of Hangal et al. (2010). In that method, each directed edge carries an influence weight: the share of one node's total interaction investment that goes to the other node. The method then picks the path that minimises log(1/D) plus the log of 1 over the product of edge influences, with D = 0.95. The test uses 500 random source-target pairs in each of two networks: a DBLP co-authorship subset (2001-2010, about 38.9k authors) and a 15-day Twitter retweet graph (about 23.5k users, 32k directed edges). The strongest path was longer than the shortest in 64.6% of Twitter pairs and 45.0% of DBLP pairs. Mean lengths were 6.8 vs 4.9 hops on Twitter and 4.7 vs 3.3 on DBLP. The paper calls the weighted search "better", but it reports no measure of path quality, no outcome and no significance test. What it actually shows is only that the weighted route differs from the hop route and is longer. It is a method note, not evidence about legislatures.

For Paul's systems, it matters in three places:
- **Staffer closeness router.** Its hop cost, -ln(0.8 x strength), has the same form as Hangal's per-hop log(1/D) + log(1/influence), with D = 0.8 instead of 0.95. So this paper is a method source for that router, but it gives no validation of it.
- **Social interaction layer.** Its edge probability (events divided by the author's posting volume) is essentially the paper's Eq. 3 retweet influence. The layer then averages the two directions, which throws away the asymmetry the paper argues for.
- **Dashboard recruitment path.** The path matrix PE is directed, because receiver edge multipliers and role priors make it so. But the backward Dijkstra (distToTarget) multiplies edges in the forward direction away from the target. So the chain labelled "PROVABLY-OPTIMAL" is exactly max-product only when PE is symmetric. This is UNVERIFIED (DE-062).
works.question: Does using directed, weighted influence edges (capturing asymmetry and tie strength) make social-search paths from source to target more effective than the hop-count shortest path given by Dijkstra? (Sec. 1, p.1-2; Abstract)
works.method: Descriptive comparison of two path algorithms on the same source-destination pairs. Baseline: Dijkstra shortest path, measured by hop count, ties broken at random (Sec. 4, p.5; Sec. 5.1). Comparator: influence-based strongest path (Algorithm 1, from [5]), which enumerates candidate paths, multiplies edge influences along each path, and returns the path minimizing log(1/D) + log(1/product of influences) with D = 0.95 (p.5). Edge influence: DBLP = Papers(vi,vj)/sum_k Papers(vj,vk) (Eq. 2, p.6); Twitter = Retweets(Y,X)/sum_Z Retweets(Y,Z) (Eq. 3, p.6); general form Eq. 1 (p.4). Outcome measures: path length in hops and mean influence. No significance tests.

findings.numbers: Mean influence: Twitter 0.67, DBLP 0.60

findings.numbers: Strongest > shortest: 225 of 500 (45.0%); equal: 275 of 500 (55.0%)

findings.numbers: Twitter: Avg |Pstrong| 6.8, Avg |Pshort| 4.9; DBLP: Avg |Pstrong| 4.7, Avg |Pshort| 3.3

works.title: A UAV Path Planning Algorithm Based on an Improved D* Lite Algorithm for Forest Firefighting
works.summary:
Luo et al. (2020, Chinese Automation Congress) change D* Lite for 3D firefighting-drone path planning in maps that are partly unknown. They shrink the map to a quarter of its size and search backward from the goal on that coarse map. They then refine a 40 m local window around the drone's 20 m radar range, smooth the path with sight-line pruning and a Catmull-Rom spline, and replan whenever the path is blocked or the target moves. Several targets are visited greedily, nearest first. All evidence is simulated: one run per synthetic grid, plain D* Lite as the only comparison, no variance, and a Table 1 whose time cells contradict the text for Env1 and Env2. The usable results are narrow. Path lengths are within about 8% of each other. Env3 shows a large speed gain (12.6 s vs 0.25 s), but only on a grid of about a million cells. The authors themselves conclude that plain D* Lite is fine for short-range planning where the map changes little.

For Paul's systems the paper matters for two reasons. First, his addendum names D* Lite and LPA* as the operational replanning layer. This paper suggests the benefit depends on scale: incremental and hierarchical search pays off on very large graphs. Paul's 533-member cosponsor graph is far smaller, and full recomputation there is cheap. Second, the dashboard's recruitment pathfinder already searches backward from the target, which is D* Lite's structure. works.question: Can an improved D* Lite incremental search, combined with map zooming and path smoothing, plan safe, short, real-time 3D paths for firefighting UAVs that reach suspected fire spots and UGVs (refuelling/material stations) when the 3D workspace is partly or wholly unknown?
works.method: Improved D* Lite (Sec. II.B, steps 1-7, p.4234-4235): (1) zoom the map out to a quarter of its size; (2) if Euclidean start-to-goal distance is below 28, run plain D* Lite, otherwise plan on the shrunken map with reverse search from the target; (3) scan obstacles with radar range r = 20 m and refine a local window d = 2r = 40 m; (4) smooth the path with two methods: sight-line node removal (method 1) and centripetal Catmull-Rom spline insertion (method 2); (5) fill the trajectory where node coordinates differ by more than 1 on any axis; (6) re-plan when the path is invalidated (next node more than r away, or target moved). works.title: An Improved D* Lite-Based Dynamic Route Planning Algorithm for Ships in Arctic Waters
works.summary:
Xu et al. (2024) change D* Lite so that a ship's route can be re-planned cheaply as Arctic ice changes. The test grid is 448 x 304 cells at 25 km. They make three changes: (1) a local-update rule, where a cell that becomes blocked keeps its old cost and a cell that opens takes its new cost, so changes don't spread across the whole map; (2) a path-extraction rule that picks the unexplored successor with the lowest c+g, which avoids deadlocks at the edge of updated regions; (3) shortcut smoothing. Cost is a weighted sum, delta*risk + distance.

Compared with the original D* Lite, nodes updated fell 34.9% in the freezing period (18,468 vs 28,351) and 79.5% in the melting period. Planning time fell 46% and 86%. Route length stayed within about 0.1%, and average risk was unchanged. Raising delta trades length for risk (freezing period: R 0.076 to 0.039, distance +3.4%). Each period is one simulated voyage, with no variance and no hardware stated. Some numbers in the text don't match the tables: 8 cells x 25 km is about 108 n mi, not 432, and the 0.07% error figure can't be reproduced.

For Paul's systems the paper is narrow. None of the router code (fec/) has D* Lite or LPA*. The gains need large graphs where repeated queries see small, local changes. The 533-node cosponsor graph is too small for incremental replanning to matter, and the staffer router serves many different origin/target pairs. Its approximate local update would also break Paul's 2026-10-03 rule that staffer routes must be exactly optimal. The paper's sharpest use is diagnostic. Its warning that extracting a path from stale cost-to-goal values can deadlock describes the dashboard's buildPath "member dropped" mode: distToTarget ignores dropped members, but tracePath skips them, so the chain labelled "PROVABLY-OPTIMAL" is not optimal once someone is dropped (UNVERIFIED, read from the code but not run). The paper also shows that scenario.py's D* Lite citation claims a reuse of earlier work that the code doesn't do.
works.question: How can D* Lite dynamic replanning be made cheap enough for real-time ship routing in Arctic waters, where ice conditions change over large areas, while keeping route distance and average risk close to full re-planning? The authors set the goal as cutting node updates and planning time without changing the heuristic.
works.method: Improved D* Lite with three modified rules. (1) Local update (Sec. 2.2, Eq. 5, Algorithm 1): a node that becomes an obstacle takes its cost from the old data, and a node that becomes navigable takes its cost from the new data, so updates do not spread through the whole map. (2) Path extraction (Sec. 2.3, Eq. 6, Algorithm 2): the next node is the unexplored successor minimizing c + g, which avoids deadlocks at the boundary of updated regions. (3) Path optimization (Sec. 2.4, Eqs. 7-9): shortcut any segment where the direct connection costs less and has no obstacles. Risk r = h x C / Icemax (Eq. 10); cost = delta*r + d (Eq. 12); average route risk R = sum(r_i d_i)/sum(d_i) (Eq. 13). Non-navigable cells are land, cells with average ice thickness above Icemax, and cells with r above the threshold (Sec. 3.1). Benchmarks: global re-planning every update, and the original D* Lite. All three run on identical ice snapshots and ship positions.

findings.finding: Freezing period, improved vs original D* Lite: nodes updated fell by 34.9% (18,468 vs 28,351); planning time fell by 46.2% (924 s vs 1,720 s). Voyage distance 2,558.7 vs 2,561.4 n mi; average risk identical at 0.076.
Freezing period, improved vs global re-planning: nodes updated fell 74.6% and planning time fell 72.7%. Route quality matched global re-planning on risk, with distance within about 0.1%.
Melting period, improved vs original D* Lite: nodes updated fell 79.5% and planning time fell 85.7%. Voyage distance 2,419.1 vs 2,418.1 n mi; risk identical at 0.615.
Melting period, improved vs global re-planning: nodes updated fell 85.3% and planning time fell 86.7%.

Sensitivity, freezing period: raising Icemax from 1.0 to 1.4 m shortens the route (2,654.5 to 2,459.9 n mi) and raises average risk (0.002 to 0.113). Raising delta from 1 to 3 at 1.2 m lengthens the route (2,558.7 to 2,645.5 n mi) and lowers risk (0.076 to 0.039).

Sensitivity, melting period: delta 1 to 3 at 2.8 m lengthens the route (2,419.1 to 2,644.1 n mi) and lowers risk (0.615 to 0.468). Risk does not fall monotonically with Icemax: at delta 1 it is 0.625, 0.631, 0.615 for 2.4, 2.6, 2.8 m.

works.title: Multi-Objective Path-Based D* Lite
works.summary: Ren, Rathinam, Likhachev and Choset (RA-L 2022) present MOPBD*, an incremental planner that keeps the full Pareto-optimal path set between a moving start and a fixed goal when edge cost vectors change. It merges D* Lite's reuse of earlier search (g and v values, local consistency) with NAMOA*'s path-based expansion, so each node stores a set of non-dominated cost vectors rather than one value. Theorem 1 claims the stored set equals the true Pareto front on termination. An epsilon-dominance variant trims those sets and trades accuracy for speed. The tests use simulated 4-connected grids from the Stern et al. MAPF benchmark, with random integer costs, 2 to 4 objectives, Python code, obstacles inserted every 7 moves, and 1 to 5 minute limits. Against the node-based incremental MOD*, MOPBD* is faster by up to an order of magnitude with two objectives. Against NAMOA* from scratch it needs fewer expansions but is not always faster: it is slower on the 16x16 empty map, and at four objectives from-scratch NAMOA* wins. The worst case can exceed from-scratch search when many states are invalidated. In Melange, cosponsor_route.py names MOPBD* in its docstring but does not implement it. It builds greedy recruitment sets under five fixed risk weights and then filters the points by dominance. That is a weighted-sum sweep over a set-selection problem, not a Pareto search over source-target paths, and it never replans incrementally. The paper's main use for Melange is as a yardstick that shows this gap. A second use is a possible two-objective view of the staffer route cost, which currently folds strength and uncertainty into one weighted sum. This analysis is UNVERIFIED (DE-062).
works.question: How to incrementally recompute the full Pareto-optimal path set in a graph whose multi-objective edge costs change during robot navigation, by fusing D* Lite reuse with NAMOA* path-based expansion.
works.method: Algorithm design plus simulation benchmark, implemented in Python. Simulator: planner computes the Pareto set; robot follows a random path from it; every k=7 moves an obstacle node (incident edges set to infinite cost) is added ahead; planner replans. Baselines: MOD* (node-based incremental) and NAMOA* from scratch. MOPBD*-epsilon compared with NAMOA*-epsilon, epsilon in {0.01, 0.02, 0.05}. Heuristic: unit vector scaled by Manhattan distance. Correctness argued by Theorem 1 (proof, no numerical check); worst-case runtime argued analytically. No statistical testing.

works.title: Conflict-Based Search for Multi-Agent Path Planning Using D*Lite for Dynamic Re-planning: Analysis and Verification
works.summary:
Abdel-Rahman et al. (2025) swap A* for D* Lite as the low-level single-agent planner inside Conflict-Based Search (CBS), a two-level multi-agent path-finding method. They test it on simulated 3D voxel grids with moving or appearing obstacles. In the paper's Table 2 averages, execution time falls from 5.575 s to 0.04 s and nodes explored fall from 2142 to 250.5, while D* Lite paths come out about 0.8% longer (15.73 vs 15.6). The paper labels that change -0.8% and says optimality is kept. The evidence is thin:
- The number of runs is not reported, and there is no variance or significance test.
- The 5.575 s average does not match its own Table 1, whose values average to 4.575 s.
- The node reduction comes entirely from the 4-neighbour case. With 8 neighbours, D* Lite explores more nodes than A* (198 vs 178).
- The scalability claim rests on one 15-agent case.
- Nothing in the paper concerns legislators, lobbying or social networks.

For Paul's systems, the paper is relevant only to path-finding, as a possible design pattern rather than as evidence. D* Lite earns its speed by reusing earlier search work when edge costs change. None of the built routers do that: the cosponsor route finder, the dashboard recruitment chain and the staffer route search each rebuild every search from scratch on a fixed graph. On a 533-member graph a full recompute is already cheap, so the paper's compute savings do not transfer. Its useful idea is conceptual. When a planned recruitment ask fails or a member's stance changes, the route should be repaired, not abandoned. The dashboard's chain-hold figure currently assumes no rerouting at all. Paul's addendum makes D* Lite and LPA* the operational layer, and this paper is too weak to support that choice on its own.
works.question: Does replacing A* with D* Lite as the low-level single-agent planner inside Conflict-Based Search (CBS) reduce computation time and nodes explored, while keeping path length, for multi-agent path finding in dynamic environments (moving or appearing obstacles, moving agents)?
works.method: Simulation comparison of two low-level planners inside CBS: A* (baseline CBS-A*) versus D* Lite (CBS-D*Lite), each with 4-point (4 directions in 3D) and 8-point (4 plus diagonals) neighbour search. Pseudocode is in Fig. 1 (p.23). Metrics: execution time (s) to compute paths for all agents, nodes explored (expansions by the low-level planner), and average path length per agent (units). Results are reported as means across test scenarios (Table 2) with per-case values for 15 agents (Table 1). Qualitative claims on adaptability, conflict-resolution responsiveness and scalability are drawn from the same runs (p.28). No replication count, variance, confidence intervals or significance tests are reported. Implementation language, hardware and random seeds are not stated.
